questiontext.text: Draft problem: A peer says the ending is unclear because the reader cannot tell why the character leaves. What is the best next step?

answer.text: Add or revise a moment that shows the character's reason for leaving.
Ignore the feedback because all endings are confusing.

questiontext.text: Workshop context: Which feedback is most useful?

answer.text: I do not like stories like this.
The repeated hallway image builds tension; consider clarifying what the character fears at the end.

questiontext.text: Format context: A script has dialogue but no character labels. What should be revised?

answer.text: Add clear speaker labels and useful stage directions.

questiontext.text: Which answer best explains author craft reasoning?

answer.text: I placed the final image on its own line so the reader pauses before the speaker's decision.

questiontext.text: Which piece is most publication-ready?

answer.text: A story with random spacing and no review.
A revised poem with purposeful line breaks, checked conventions, clear title, and appropriate content.

questiontext.text: Feedback says a paragraph is confusing because two speakers are in one paragraph. Which revision best fits?

answer.text: Start a new paragraph when the speaker changes and check dialogue tags.

questiontext.text: Which answer should be eliminated first?

answer.text: Consider feedback and protect the writer's purpose.

questiontext.text: A portfolio note should include what?

answer.text: Selection reason, revision evidence, and final readiness explanation.

questiontext.text: Which is the best author presentation opening?

answer.text: I will tell the whole plot first.
I do not know why I wrote it.
"Open Door" is a short story meant to show a character deciding whether to trust someone again.

questiontext.text: Which revision most directly improves reader effect?

answer.text: Replacing "I was sad" with an image of the last bus passing without stopping.

questiontext.text: What is active listening in workshop?

answer.text: Restating the writer's purpose before giving feedback.

questiontext.text: Which is a strong publication decision?

answer.text: Use a school-appropriate excerpt and remove private identifying details.

questiontext.text: Which statement best separates revision and polishing?

answer.text: Revision improves meaning or structure; polishing checks final details.
Polishing should happen before reading the draft.

questiontext.text: A poem uses random line breaks that make the central image hard to read. What should the writer do?

answer.text: Revise line breaks so the image and pauses support the intended effect.
Keep the random breaks because all poems must be confusing.

questiontext.text: Which response best explains a revision decision?

answer.text: I changed it because I had to.
I shortened the ending because feedback showed the first version explained too much.

questiontext.text: Which feedback is least helpful?

answer.text: What does the character want in the final scene?
Consider adding one sound before the reveal.

questiontext.text: Which checklist best fits Unit 5?

answer.text: Understand purpose, consider feedback, revise, check format and conventions, prepare readers, explain author reasoning.

questiontext.text: A writer's presentation retells every event but gives no craft reasoning. What is the best correction?

answer.text: Focus on purpose, two craft choices, and one revision decision.

questiontext.text: Which answer best handles online collaborative feedback?

answer.text: Consider suggestions, accept what improves the piece, and reject what conflicts with purpose.

questiontext.text: Which convention issue should be fixed before publication?

answer.text: A purposeful line break in a poem.
Dialogue punctuation that makes speakers hard to follow.

questiontext.text: Which selection rationale is strongest?

answer.text: I selected this story because revision from feedback clarified the character's decision and made the ending stronger.
I selected this because it was first in my folder.
I selected this because I did not read the others.
I selected this because it has no title.

questiontext.text: Which answer best identifies reader effect?

answer.text: The shorter sentence slows the reader at the final decision.

questiontext.text: Which is the strongest response to vague feedback?

answer.text: Ask for the specific place where the reader became confused.

questiontext.text: Which author note is best for publication?

answer.text: This piece is about everything and nothing.
This poem uses the bus stop image to show waiting; I revised the final line so the speaker's choice is clearer.

questiontext.text: Which response shows Unit 5 mastery?

answer.text: I can type a rough draft and stop.
I can use feedback to revise, check format and conventions, prepare work for publication, and explain craft choices to an audience.

questiontext.text: Draft Excerpt: I walked into the room. It was weird. Something felt different. Feedback: I cannot picture the room. Which revision goal is best?

answer.text: Change every sentence because the draft is bad.
Add one specific detail that helps readers picture the room.
Delete the whole draft and start over.
Add a new character with no connection to the room.

questiontext.text: Draft Excerpt: The poem is about missing my old neighborhood. Feedback: Add one concrete image from the neighborhood. Which revision best uses the feedback?

answer.text: Add the image of the corner store sign flickering after rain.
Add a sentence saying the poem is emotional.
Change the poem into a research report.

questiontext.text: Feedback: Make it better. How should this feedback be classified?
Draft Sentence: Mara handed Lena the box after she dropped it, and it made her upset. Which revision is clearest?

answer.text: She handed it over after it happened and it was upsetting.
After Maya opened the box, she handed the old photograph to Lena.
The box was there and it was a thing.
They did it and then it happened.

questiontext.text: Draft: The rain stopped. I found the letter. The house was quiet. Which revision improves cohesion?

answer.text: The rain stopped. I found the letter. The house was quiet.
When the rain stopped, I found the letter on the quiet porch.

questiontext.text: Workshop context: A writer says, "I want this scene to feel tense but still clear." Which response best shows active listening?

answer.text: You want the scene to create tension while the reader can still follow what is happening.

questiontext.text: Workshop context: A peer draft uses the line, "The porch light held its breath." Which feedback best names a craft strength?

answer.text: You should write about a different house.
The personification of the porch light creates a quiet, tense mood.

questiontext.text: Draft Excerpt: I waited outside the rehearsal room. The music stopped. I raised my hand to knock, then lowered it. The writer wants a poem that emphasizes hesitation. Which format choice best fits?

answer.text: Put the entire draft in one long line.
Use line breaks around "raised my hand" and "lowered it" so the reader pauses with the speaker.

questiontext.text: Draft Excerpt: "Come in" Mara said but she did not open the door. Which prose-story revision best improves publication quality?

answer.text: "Come in," Mara said, but she did not open the door.
come in mara said but she did not open the door
COME IN MARA SAID BUT SHE DID NOT OPEN THE DOORfor this item

questiontext.text: Publication context: A student finishes typing a rough draft and wants to place it in the class online publication space immediately. What should happen first?

answer.text: Post it immediately because typing means it is finished.
Review purpose, feedback, format, audience appropriateness, and final conventions before publication.
Change the title only and ignore the rest.

questiontext.text: Collaborative publication context: Which role checks whether line breaks, paragraph breaks, title, and spacing fit the creative form?
Author presentation context: Which opening is strongest?

answer.text: "After the Rain" is a short prose piece meant to show a character who is safe but still unsure how to move forward.
My story has a driveway, rain, and an umbrella, and then things happen.
I do not know what my piece is about.
The audience should figure out everything with no help.

questiontext.text: Which sentence best explains craft reasoning?

answer.text: I used an umbrella because umbrellas exist.
I repeated the umbrella image so the reader could see the character holding onto protection even after the rain stopped.
I made choices because writing needs choices.

questiontext.text: Portfolio context: A writer chooses a story only because it is the shortest draft. What is the best correction?

answer.text: Choose it automatically because short always means portfolio-ready.
Choose the first draft found and skip revision.
Choose a piece because it shows growth, strong craft, or clear publication potential.
Choose no piece because portfolios cannot include creative work.

questiontext.text: A draft has a confusing ending and several spelling errors. What should the writer address first?

answer.text: Correct spelling only and ignore the ending.
Revise the ending so the reader understands the character's decision.
